claim: Male germ cells of all placental mammals express an ancient nuclear RNA binding protein called RBMXL2.
source: Male germ cells of all placental mammals express an ancient nuclear RNA binding protein of unknown function called RBMXL2.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by the evolutionary analysis showing RBMXL2 is found in all placental mammals.

claim: Deletion of the retrogene encoding RBMXL2 blocks spermatogenesis.
source: Here we find that deletion of the retrogene encoding RBMXL2 blocks spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from the knockout mouse model.

claim: RBMXL2 controls splicing patterns during meiosis.
source: Transcriptome analyses of age-matched deletion mice show that RBMXL2 controls splicing patterns during meiosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNAseq data showing splicing changes in Rbmxl2-/- mice.

claim: RBMXL2 represses the selection of aberrant splice sites.
source: In particular, RBMXL2 represses the selection of aberrant splice sites and the insertion of cryptic and premature terminal exons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNAseq data showing increased cryptic splice site usage in knockout mice.

claim: RBMXL2 represses the insertion of cryptic and premature terminal exons.
source: In particular, RBMXL2 represses the selection of aberrant splice sites and the insertion of cryptic and premature terminal exons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNAseq data showing increased cryptic exon inclusion in knockout mice.

claim: A Rbmxl2 retrogene has been conserved across mammals.
source: Our data suggest a Rbmxl2 retrogene has been conserved across mammals as part of a splicing control mechanism that is fundamentally important to germ cell biology.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by evolutionary analysis showing RBMXL2 presence in all placental mammals.

claim: The RBMXL2 mechanism buffers high ambient concentrations of splicing activators during meiosis.
source: We propose that this mechanism is essential to meiosis because it buffers the high ambient concentrations of splicing activators, thereby preventing poisoning of key transcripts and disruption to gene expression by aberrant splice site selection.
evidence: This is proposed in the abstract based on the observed splicing defects and is supported by in vitro experiments showing RBMXL2 can antagonize Tra2β activity.

claim: There are extremely high levels of transcription and transcriptome complexity in testicular cells.
source: It has been a long recognised hallmark of mammalian gene expression patterns that there are extremely high levels of transcription and transcriptome complexity in testicular cells (de la Grange et al., 2010; Licatalosi, 2016; Soumillon et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008; Clark et al., 2007; Grosso et al., 2008; Yeo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: High gene expression levels in testis result from epigenetic changes that favour relaxed patterns of gene expression during meiosis.
source: These high gene expression levels are thought to result from epigenetic changes that favour relaxed patterns of gene expression during meiosis – the unique form of division used to generate sperm and eggs (Soumillon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Many nuclear RNA-binding proteins are differentially expressed during and immediately after meiosis.
source: Many nuclear RNA-binding proteins are differentially expressed during and immediately after meiosis (Grellscheid et al., 2011; Schmid et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: RBMXL2 is expressed only during and immediately after male meiosis, but not in the preceding spermatogonial cells.
source: These include the nuclear RNA binding protein RBMXL2 (also known as hnRNP GT) that is expressed only during and immediately after male meiosis, but not in the preceding spermatogonial cells (Ehrmann et al., 2008) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation and supported by Figure 1A showing expression pattern.

claim: Point mutations within the human chromosome 11 RBMXL2 gene have been identified in infertile men.
source: Consistent with an important function in germ cell development, genetic studies have identified point mutations within infertile men in the human chromosome 11 RBMXL2 gene (Westerveld et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: RBMXL2 belongs to the same gene family as RBMY.
source: A further connection to male infertility is that RBMXL2 belongs to the same gene family as RBMY, which was historically the first human Y chromosome infertility gene identified in the search for the AZF (AZOOSPERMIA FACTOR) gene (Ma et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: RBMY was historically the first human Y chromosome infertility gene identified in the search for the AZF gene.
source: A further connection to male infertility is that RBMXL2 belongs to the same gene family as RBMY, which was historically the first human Y chromosome infertility gene identified in the search for the AZF (AZOOSPERMIA FACTOR) gene (Ma et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: RBMXL2 evolved approximately 65 million years ago via retrotransposition of an mRNA from the X chromosome located RBMX gene.
source: RBMXL2 evolved ~65 million years ago via retrotransposition of an mRNA from the X chromosome located RBMX gene (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by Figure 1A showing the evolutionary relationship.

claim: An RBMXL2 gene is found in all placental mammals.
source: An RBMXL2 gene is found in all placental mammals, which is consistent with a fundamental role in germ cell biology.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by evolutionary analysis.

claim: RBMXL2 protein has an N-terminal RNA Recognition Motif (RRM).
source: This role remains to be identified, but RBMXL2 protein has an N-terminal RNA Recognition Motif (abbreviated RRM, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RBMX and RBMY proteins are very similar to RBMXL2 with 73.2% and 36.8% overall identity respectively.
source: RBMX and RBMY proteins are also nuclear RNA binding proteins that are very similar to RBMXL2 (73.2% and 36.8% overall identity to RBMX and RBMY, respectively; 93.7% and 77.2% identity within the RRMs, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: RBMX and RBMY proteins have 93.7% and 77.2% identity to RBMXL2 within the RRMs.
source: RBMX and RBMY proteins are also nuclear RNA binding proteins that are very similar to RBMXL2 (73.2% and 36.8% overall identity to RBMX and RBMY, respectively; 93.7% and 77.2% identity within the RRMs, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both RBMX and RBMY proteins bind to AA dinucleotide-containing RNA sequences.
source: The RNA binding specificity of RBMXL2 protein is unknown, but both RBMX and RBMY proteins bind to AA dinucleotide-containing RNA sequences (Cléry et al., 2011; Moursy et al., 2014; Nasim et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: RBMXL2, RBMX and RBMY proteins interact with and modulate the splicing activity of Tra2β and SR proteins in vitro.
source: The RBMXL2, RBMX and RBMY proteins interact with and modulate the splicing activity of Tra2β and SR proteins in vitro (Figure 1B) (Cléry et al., 2011; Moursy et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2009; Nasim et al., 2003; Elliott et al., 2000a), suggesting a role in splicing control.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations and Figure 1B.

claim: Deletion of the splicing regulator protein PTBP2 within germ cells affects mRNA isoforms important for cell-cell communication with Sertoli cells.
source: For example, deletion of the splicing regulator protein PTBP2 within germ cells affects mRNA isoforms important for cell-cell communication with Sertoli cells (Hannigan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Some alternative splicing events in the testis are conserved between humans and mice.
source: Some alternative splicing events in the testis are conserved between humans and mice so may control fundamental aspects of germ cell biology (Schmid et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Many alternative splicing patterns are not conserved between humans and mice.
source: However many alternative splicing patterns are not conserved between humans and mice (Kan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: RBMX protein is reported to control transcription.
source: RBMX protein is also reported to control transcription (Takemoto et al., 2007), affect DNA double strand repair and mitotic sister chromatid cohesion (Adamson et al., 2012; Matsunaga et al., 2012), and to bind to m6A methylated RNA (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: RBMX protein affects DNA double strand repair and mitotic sister chromatid cohesion.
source: RBMX protein is also reported to control transcription (Takemoto et al., 2007), affect DNA double strand repair and mitotic sister chromatid cohesion (Adamson et al., 2012; Matsunaga et al., 2012), and to bind to m6A methylated RNA (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: RBMX protein binds to m6A methylated RNA.
source: RBMX protein is also reported to control transcription (Takemoto et al., 2007), affect DNA double strand repair and mitotic sister chromatid cohesion (Adamson et al., 2012; Matsunaga et al., 2012), and to bind to m6A methylated RNA (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Men carrying the AZFb deletion on their Y chromosomes are missing RBMY genes and undergo meiotic arrest.
source: Men carrying the AZFb deletion on their Y chromosomes are missing RBMY genes and undergo meiotic arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: It is unclear if RBMY loss is causing the AZFb deletion phenotype, because the deletion interval encompasses several other genes which could contribute to male infertility.
source: However, it is unclear if RBMY loss is causing this phenotype, because the deletion interval encompasses several other genes which could contribute to male infertility (Elliott, 2000; Vogt et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The RBMX and RBMY genes are transcriptionally inactivated within the XY body during meiotic and immediately post-meiotic germ cells.
source: Within the meiotic and immediately post-meiotic germ cells which express RBMXL2, the RBMX and RBMY genes are transcriptionally inactivated within a heterochromatic structure called the XY body (Wang, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: No RBMXL2 protein is made within Rbmxl2-/- adult testis.
source: We confirmed deletion of this genomic region in homozygous Rbmxl2 gene knockout (Rbmxl2-/-) mice by Southern blotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and the specific absence of the 50 KDa RBMXL2 protein from knockout testes by Western blotting (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C Western blot.

claim: Rbmxl2-/- mice developed comparably to their wild type littermates but their testes were much smaller.
source: Rbmxl2-/- mice developed comparably to their wild type littermates but their testes were much smaller (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Adult Rbmxl2-/- mice contained cells undergoing meiosis but almost no post-meiotic cells.
source: This small testis phenotype correlated with a severe disruption of testicular histology. Adult Rbmxl2-/- mice contained cells undergoing meiosis but almost no post-meiotic cells (Figure 2C, meiotic spermatocytes are abbreviated Spc, and post-meiotic round spermatids are abbreviated Rtd).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C histology.

claim: The epididymis dissected from Rbmxl2-/- mice were completely devoid of sperm.
source: The epididymis dissected from Rbmxl2-/- mice were completely devoid of sperm. Four wild type mice tested had an average of 7.07 ± 1.39×106 epididymal sperm ml−1, compared with zero in four Rbmxl2-/- mice (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: No effect on female fertility was observed in Rbmxl2-/- mice.
source: No effect on female fertility was observed in Rbmxl2-/- mice (not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental observation.

claim: Very rarely a few round spermatids were observed in adult Rbmxl2-/- testis sections.
source: Very rarely a few round spermatids were observed in adult Rbmxl2-/- testis sections (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), although no elongated spermatids were detected.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 21dpp there were significantly fewer round spermatids in the Rbmxl2-/- sections compared to wild type.
source: At 21dpp there were still significantly fewer round spermatids in the Rbmxl2-/- sections compared to wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), even though there would have been less time for round spermatid cell death compared with the adult.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rbmxl2-/- mice arrest germ cell development during the diplotene substage of meiotic prophase.
source: Staining of nuclear spreads with antibodies specific to the meiotic chromosome proteins SYCP1 and SYCP3 more precisely showed that Rbmxl2-/- mice arrest germ cell development during the diplotene substage of meiotic prophase (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Metaphase I nuclei were only detected in wild type mice and not in Rbmxl2-/- mice.
source: Metaphase I nuclei were only detected in wild type mice and not in Rbmxl2-/- mice (N = 3 wild type and N = 3 Rbmxl2-/-testes, 180 and 138 spermatocyte nuclei scored for wild type and Rbmxl2-/- respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on quantitative analysis of nuclear spreads.

claim: No significant differences in the frequency of earlier stages of meiotic prophase were detected between Rbmxl2-/- and wild type testes.
source: No significant differences in the frequency of earlier stages of meiotic prophase were detected between Rbmxl2-/- and wild type testes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on quantitative analysis.

claim: Adult Rbmxl2-/- germ cells die via apoptosis.
source: Staining of adult testis sections with PAS or antibodies specific to the apoptotic marker activated Caspase three further showed that adult Rbmxl2-/- germ cells die via apoptosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E–F.

claim: There was a decreased number of H3K9me3-marked centromere clusters in Rbmxl2-/- diplotene nuclei.
source: Analysis of diplotene nuclear spreads revealed further abnormalities in the Rbmxl2-/- testis. There was a decreased number of H3K9me3-marked centromere clusters (Takada et al., 2011), with each individual cluster also containing more centromeres than in wild type testis (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C.

claim: H3K9me3 staining was present at the sex body in 82% of wild type diplotene spermatocytes, but essentially absent in mutant diplotene spermatocytes (1.5%).
source: H3K9me3 staining was also present at the sex body in a proportion (82%) of wild type diplotene spermatocytes, but essentially absent in mutant diplotene spermatocytes (1.5% of diplotene spermatocytes stained, 66 Rbmxl2-/- and 66 wild type nuclei scored, n = 3 for both) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Asynapsis was rarely observed in either control or mutant pachytene stage spermatocytes.
source: Asynapsis was rarely observed in either control or mutant pachytene stage spermatocytes, indicating that the defect causing diplotene arrest does not significantly impact either synaptonemal complex formation or meiotic homology searching (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E) (N = 3, 109 and 94 nuclei scored for wild type and Rbmxl2-/- respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E.

claim: Overall patterns of transcription were similar between wild type and Rbmxl2-/- 18dpp testes.
source: Gene expression analysis of this RNAseq data (Anders and Huber, 2010) showed overall patterns of transcription were similar between wild type and Rbmxl2-/- 18dpp testes (Figure 3A, and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Only 45 genes showed a fold change greater or equal to two between the wild type and Rbmxl2-/- testes, with an adjusted p value of less than 0.05.
source: Only 45 genes showed a fold change greater or equal to two between the wild type and Rbmxl2-/- testes, with an adjusted p value of less than 0.05, and only 23 of these changes were for known protein coding genes (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on RNAseq analysis.

claim: The strongest difference in overall gene expression between the wild type and Rbmxl2-/- backgrounds was for the Rbmxl2-/- gene itself.
source: The strongest difference in overall gene expression between the wild type and Rbmxl2-/- backgrounds was for the Rbmxl2-/- gene itself, as expected since the Rbmxl2-/- gene is deleted from the knockout mouse.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on RNAseq analysis.

claim: Strong expression changes were detected within the Fsip2 gene, particularly for Fsip2 exon 16 and downstream exons that were expressed only in the wild type background.
source: We also detected strong expression changes within the Fsip2 gene, particularly for Fsip2 exon 16 and downstream exons that were expressed only in the wild type background (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: A total of 237 high-confidence, mis-regulated local splicing variations were identified in 186 genes.
source: We carried out further bioinformatic analysis to specifically search for mis-regulated splicing events in the Rbmxl2-/- testes (Vaquero-Garcia et al., 2016). A total of 237 high-confidence, mis-regulated local splicing variations were identified in 186 genes (Figure 3B, and Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MAJIQ analysis and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 23 out of 27 tested splicing changes were experimentally validated using RT-PCR.
source: Using RT-PCR to distinguish splice isoforms 27 of these splicing changes were experimentally tested, validating 23/27 splice isoform switches (Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on RT-PCR validation experiments.

claim: Whole gene deletion of 25 out of 186 RBMXL2-regulated genes cause male infertility.
source: Analysis of knockout phenotypes provided by the MGD (Smith et al., 2018) indicated that whole gene deletion of 25/186 RBMXL2-regulated genes cause male infertility. These latter target genes must thus have a key role in germ cell development (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 6, Figure 3—source data 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MGD database analysis.

claim: Each of the top 10 5-mers from RBMXL2 HITS-CLIP contained the dinucleotide AA.
source: Enriched motif analysis of the sequenced RBMXL2 CLIP tags showed that each of the top 10 5-mers contained the dinucleotide AA (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: AA is the dinucleotide bound by RBMX.
source: Interestingly, AA is also the dinucleotide bound by RBMX (Moursy et al., 2014), which is consistent with over 90% shared sequence identity within the RRMs of these proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: RBMXL2 cross-linked sites mapped to the mouse genome most frequently within introns.
source: These intragenic cross-linked sites mapped to the mouse genome most frequently within introns, consistent with RBMXL2 being involved in nuclear RNA-processing events (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Enrichment of RBMXL2 binding was observed both within alternative exon sequences and in regions proximal to regulated splice sites compared to non-regulated events.
source: We observed enrichment of RBMXL2 binding both within alternative exon sequences and in regions proximal to regulated splice sites compared to non-regulated events (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 60% of the 87 most easily visualised classical splicing events controlled by RBMXL2 involve the altered selection of de-novo splice sites.
source: This showed that 60% of the 87 most easily visualised classical splicing events controlled by RBMXL2 involve the altered selection of de-novo splice sites (defined as not currently annotated on the most recent build of the Mus musculus genome GRCm38/mm10, Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of RNAseq data.

claim: 84% of cryptic exons repressed by RBMXL2 were either not multiples of three or introduced stop codons into their mRNAs.
source: Detailed investigation indicated 84% of such cryptic exons were either not multiples of three or introduced stop codons into their mRNAs, meaning their insertion into mRNAs would disrupt protein reading frames and interfere with meiotic protein expression.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of cryptic exons.

claim: High inclusion of a cryptic terminal exon was detected within the 5′ UTR of the Kdm4d gene in Rbmxl2-/- testes.
source: Splicing inclusion of cryptic terminal exons could also severely impact patterns of meiotic gene expression. We detected high inclusion of a cryptic terminal exon within the 5′ UTR of the Kdm4d gene (Figure 4A and B, note also increased splicing of an already annotated upstream Kdm4d alternative exon within the Rbmxl2-/- testis).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Kdm4d encodes a histone demethylase protein that is important for normal patterns of germ cell apoptosis in the testis.
source: Kdm4d encodes a histone demethylase protein that is important for normal patterns of germ cell apoptosis in the testis (Iwamori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Some individual RNAseq reads extended past the 5′ splice site of the Kdm4d cryptic exon and then terminated downstream following a consensus polyadenylation site (AATAAA) sequence.
source: Consistent with this, some individual RNAseq reads extended past the 5′ splice site of the Kdm4d cryptic exon and then terminated downstream following a consensus polyadenylation site (AATAAA) sequence (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 18 additional splicing events that mapped to terminal exons showed increased selection in the Rbmxl2-/- testes.
source: We also detected increased selection in the Rbmxl2-/- testes of another 17 splicing events that mapped to terminal exons (Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on RNAseq analysis.

claim: Loss of RBMXL2 protein activated splicing selection of individual cryptic 5′ and 3′ splice sites within introns that increased the length of already annotated exons.
source: In addition to splicing of entire cryptic exons, loss of RBMXL2 protein also activated splicing selection of individual cryptic 5′ and 3′ splice sites within introns that increased the length of already annotated exons (Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on RNAseq analysis.

claim: A dip in RNAseq density for the interior of Meioc exon five was observed in the Rbmxl2-/- testis transcriptome.
source: Amongst the genes known to be important for meiosis, we observed a dip in RNAseq density for the interior of Meioc (meiosis specific gene with coiled coil domain) exon five in the Rbmxl2-/- testis transcriptome (Figure 5A) (Abby et al., 2016; Soh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the Rbmxl2-/- testes approximately 28% of the splice junctions joined Meioc exon four to an exon-internal cryptic 3′ splice site within Meioc exon 5.
source: Sashimi plots showed that in the Rbmxl2-/-testes ~ 28% of the splice junctions joined Meioc exon four to an exon-internal cryptic 3′ splice site within Meioc exon 5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A cryptic 5′ splice site within Meioc exon five was used in 22% of the Rbmxl2-/- testis transcripts.
source: A further cryptic 5′ splice site within Meioc exon five was also used in 22% of the Rbmxl2-/- testis transcripts.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on Sashimi plot analysis.

claim: Use of both cryptic splice sites converted Meioc exon five into an exitron.
source: Use of both cryptic splice sites converted Meioc exon five into an exitron (an exon with internal splice sites) (Marquez et al., 2015; Sibley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations defining exitrons.

claim: The cryptic splice sites within Meioc exon five are hardly ever used in the wild type 18dpp testis transcriptome.
source: The cryptic splice sites within Meioc exon five are hardly ever used in the wild type 18dpp testis transcriptome.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on RNAseq analysis.

claim: The internal cryptic 5′ splice site within Meioc exon five is weak compared to 5′ splice sites for other known alternative exons (7.5th percentile).
source: In silico analysis showed that the internal cryptic 5′ splice site within Meioc exon five is weak compared to 5′ splice sites for other known alternative exons (7.5th percentile by SROOGLE, compared to 57th percentile for the downstream annotated 3′ splice site (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) (Schwartz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The first two nucleotide positions downstream of the Meioc exon 5 cryptic internal 5′ splice site are GC, diverging from the GT consensus.
source: The first two nucleotide positions downstream of the Meioc exon 5- cryptic internal 5′ splice site are GC, so diverge from the GT consensus which is found flanking almost all eukaryotic introns.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence analysis.

claim: Meioc exon five is directly bound by RBMXL2 protein, evidenced by three internal HITS-CLIP tags.
source: Meioc exon five is also directly bound by RBMXL2 protein, evidenced by three internal HITS-CLIP tags (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A CLIP tag directly overlaps the Meioc exon 5 internal cryptic 5' splice site.
source: These include a CLIP tag directly overlapping the Meioc exon 5 internal cryptic 5' splice site, as well as CLIP tags upstream of the internal 3′ splice site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on HITS-CLIP data.

claim: Meioc exon five is highly conserved across species.
source: Meioc exon five is highly conserved across species suggesting it encodes a functionally important part of Meioc protein (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A conservation track.

claim: Western blotting detected a 40–50 KDa Meioc protein within the Rbmxl2-/- testis, but not in wild type or heterozygote Rbmxl2 ± testes.
source: We thus predicted that a shorter Meioc protein isoform may be produced in the Rbmxl2-/- testis. Consistent with this, Western blotting with a Meioc specific antiserum (Abby et al., 2016) detected a 40–50 KDa Meioc protein within the Rbmxl2-/- testis, but not in wild type or heterozygote Rbmxl2 ±testes (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: This 40–50 KDa molecular weight corresponds to an expected Meioc protein size following complete exitron removal.
source: This 40–50 KDa molecular weight corresponds to an expected Meioc protein size following complete exitron removal.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on predicted protein size calculation.

claim: Aberrant splice isoforms of Meioc exon five only appeared within Rbmxl2-/- testes from 14dpp.
source: We further analysed splicing patterns during the first wave of mouse spermatogenesis to test whether appearance of the Meioc splicing defects corresponded with the known expression window of RBMXL2 protein in meiotic prophase (Ehrmann et al., 2008). Aberrant splice isoforms of Meioc exon five only appeared within Rbmxl2-/- testes from 14dpp, and were barely visible at any time point within similar age wild type testes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on time-course RT-PCR analysis.

claim: Brca2 exon 11 splicing was normal at 13dpp in the Rbmxl2-/- testes, with defects appearing only during and after 14dpp.
source: RT-PCR analysis during the first wave of spermatogenesis showed Brca2 exon 11 splicing was normal at 13dpp in the Rbmxl2-/- testes, with defects appearing only during and after 14dpp (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Splicing defects in both Meioc and Brca2 appear and become progressively worse during meiotic prophase in the Rbmxl2-/- testes within genes that are expressed and processed normally in earlier germ cell types.
source: These time-course data indicate that splicing defects in both Meioc and Brca2 appear and become progressively worse during meiotic prophase in the Rbmxl2-/- testes within genes that are expressed and processed normally in earlier germ cell types.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on time-course analysis.

claim: Approximately 40% splicing inclusion of the cryptic Kdm4d exon was detected after co-transfection of the minigene into HEK293 cells with an expression vector encoding GFP.
source: We detected ~40% splicing inclusion of the cryptic Kdm4d exon after co-transfection of this minigene into HEK293 cells (that do not normally express RBMXL2) with an expression vector encoding GFP (Figure 6B lane 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Levels of Kdm4d cryptic exon splicing inclusion were repressed 6-fold upon co-transfection of a construct encoding an RBMXL2-GFP fusion protein.
source: Levels of Kdm4d cryptic exon splicing inclusion were repressed 6-fold upon co-transfection of a construct encoding an RBMXL2-GFP fusion protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on minigene assay data.

claim: RBMXL2 ΔRNP1 could still repress Kdm4d cryptic exon splicing, although slightly less efficiently than the full length RBMXL2 fusion protein.
source: We also tested the activity of an RBMXL2 fusion protein without the RNP1 motif of the RRM (RBMXL2 ΔRNP1). Consistent with RNA-protein contacts not being critical for splicing repression of this cryptic exon, RBMXL2 ΔRNP1 could still repress Kdm4d cryptic exon splicing, although slightly less efficiently than the full length RBMXL2 fusion protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on minigene assay data.

claim: Splicing of the Kdm4d cryptic exon was efficiently silenced by ectopic co-expression of an RBMX-GFP fusion protein.
source: Interestingly, splicing of the Kdm4d cryptic exon was also efficiently silenced by ectopic co-expression of an RBMX-GFP fusion protein (Figure 6B lane 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tra2β over-expression in HEK293 cells strongly increased Kdm4d cryptic exon splicing inclusion.
source: iCLIP experiments in adult mouse testis further identified the Kdm4d cryptic exon as directly binding the splicing activator protein Tra2β (Dalgliesh and Elliott, unpublished data). Consistent with this, Tra2β over-expression in HEK293 cells strongly increased Kdm4d cryptic exon splicing inclusion (Figure 6B lane 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Splicing activation by Tra2β was efficiently suppressed when the minigene was co-transfected with both RBMXL2 and Tra2β.
source: Importantly, splicing activation by Tra2β was efficiently supressed when the minigene was co-transfected at the same time with both RBMXL2 and Tra2β (Figure 6B, lanes 5 and 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cryptic exons activated in the Rbmxl2-/- testes had significantly weaker 3′ splice sites compared to their immediately adjacent downstream exons.
source: In silico analysis (Schwartz et al., 2009) of a panel of cryptic exons that were activated in the Rbmxl2-/- testes showed that these exons had significantly weaker 3′ splice sites, but similar Exonic Splicing Enhancer (ESE) sequence content compared to their immediately adjacent downstream exons (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cryptic exons activated in the Rbmxl2-/- testes had similar ESE sequence content compared to their immediately adjacent downstream exons.
source: In silico analysis (Schwartz et al., 2009) of a panel of cryptic exons that were activated in the Rbmxl2-/- testes showed that these exons had significantly weaker 3′ splice sites, but similar Exonic Splicing Enhancer (ESE) sequence content compared to their immediately adjacent downstream exons (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Loss of the ancient RBMXL2 protein completely prevents sperm production in the mouse.
source: This study finds that loss of the ancient RBMXL2 protein completely prevents sperm production in the mouse, largely because of a developmental block during meiosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the main findings.

claim: RBMXL2 protein is important to protect the meiotic transcriptome from a spectrum of splicing defects.
source: Our data further show that RBMXL2 protein is important to protect the meiotic transcriptome from a spectrum of splicing defects (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cells in meiotic prophase might be particularly susceptible to cryptic splice site poisoning because of their high levels of transcription, altered splicing regulator expression and relaxed chromatin environments.
source: Cells in meiotic prophase might be particularly susceptible to cryptic splice site poisoning because of their high levels of transcription, altered splicing regulator expression and relaxed chromatin environments (de la Grange et al., 2010; Licatalosi, 2016; Soumillon et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008; Clark et al., 2007; Grosso et al., 2008; Yeo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: The cryptic exons repressed by RBMXL2 would be poised for splicing inclusion in conditions of high concentrations of splicing activators because of their strong ESE contents.
source: In silico data suggest that the cryptic exons repressed by RBMXL2 would be poised for splicing inclusion in conditions of high concentrations of splicing activators because of their strong ESE contents.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on in silico analysis.

claim: RBMXL2 protein may buffer the activity of splicing activator proteins to prevent cryptic splice site selection from happening in meiosis.
source: We suggest a model where RBMXL2 protein may buffer the activity of splicing activator proteins to prevent such cryptic splice site selection from happening in meiosis (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 7B as a model.

claim: RBMXL2, RBMX and RBMY proteins physically interact with and antagonise the splicing activity of Tra2β and SR proteins.
source: This model is also consistent with previously reported data showing that RBMXL2, RBMX and RBMY proteins physically interact with and antagonise the splicing activity of Tra2β and SR proteins (Liu et al., 2009; Nasim et al., 2003; Venables et al., 2000; Elliott et al., 2000a) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Kdm4d cryptic exon splicing activation by Tra2β is blocked in vitro by co-expression of RBMXL2.
source: Data presented in this study also show that Kdm4d cryptic exon splicing activation by Tra2β is blocked in vitro by co-expression of RBMXL2.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing experimental results.

claim: A version of RBMXL2 deleted for the key RNP1 motif could still repress Kdm4d cryptic exon splicing, albeit slightly less efficiently than the wild type RBMXL2 protein.
source: Furthermore, a version of RBMXL2 deleted for the key RNP1 motif involved in RNA-protein interactions could still repress Kdm4d cryptic exon splicing (albeit slightly less efficiently than the wild type RBMXL2 protein).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing experimental results.

claim: Buffering protein interactions between RBMXL2 and proteins like Tra2β may be potentially more important in repressing cryptic splicing in meiosis than direct RBMXL2 RNA-protein interactions.
source: Thus buffering protein interactions between RBMXL2 and proteins like Tra2β may be potentially more important in repressing cryptic splicing in meiosis than direct RBMXL2 RNA-protein interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Loss of RBMXL2 disrupts expression of many downstream target genes in parallel, both at splicing and transcriptional levels.
source: Loss of RBMXL2 disrupts expression of many downstream target genes in parallel, both at splicing and transcriptional levels.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the findings.

claim: High levels of gene expression and alternative splicing have been observed in the nervous system.
source: High levels of gene expression and alternative splicing have also been observed in the nervous system, and this is another anatomic site where pathological cryptic exon inclusion has been reported.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as background knowledge.

claim: Neuronal cryptic exon inclusion occurs following depletion of the splicing repressor protein TDP43.
source: Neuronal cryptic exon inclusion occurs following depletion of the splicing repressor protein TDP43, and might contribute to neuron death in neurological diseases like ALS and Alzheimer's disease (Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: Cryptic splicing has been observed in cultured human cells after depletion of the splicing repressor proteins hnRNP C, hnRNPL and PTB.
source: Cryptic splicing has also been observed in cultured human cells after depletion of the splicing repressor proteins hnRNP C, hnRNPL and PTB (Ling et al., 2016; McClory et al., 2018; Zarnack et al., 2013), and in mouse oocytes depleted for the splicing factor SRSF3 (Do et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Cryptic splicing has been observed in mouse oocytes depleted for the splicing factor SRSF3.
source: Cryptic splicing has also been observed in cultured human cells after depletion of the splicing repressor proteins hnRNP C, hnRNPL and PTB (Ling et al., 2016; McClory et al., 2018; Zarnack et al., 2013), and in mouse oocytes depleted for the splicing factor SRSF3 (Do et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: RBMXL2 has a key role controlling the meiotic transcriptome.
source: Taking all these results into consideration we suggest that RBMXL2 has a key role controlling the meiotic transcriptome, and suggest that human male infertility caused by loss of RBMXL2 or its paralog RBMY may be associated with germ cell type-specific cryptic splicing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Human male infertility caused by loss of RBMXL2 or its paralog RBMY may be associated with germ cell type-specific cryptic splicing.
source: Taking all these results into consideration we suggest that RBMXL2 has a key role controlling the meiotic transcriptome, and suggest that human male infertility caused by loss of RBMXL2 or its paralog RBMY may be associated with germ cell type-specific cryptic splicing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation based on the findings.
